title: Talking to the hardware: BIOS, ports, interrupts, drivers and consoles
subtitle: MS-DOS 4.00 and FreeBSD 15.1, from IN and OUT to the terminal

slides.title: The PC as a programmer sees it
slides.subtitle: Device memory, I/O ports, interrupts
slides.notes: Start from the hardware both systems share: the same chips, the same ports, the same IRQ lines.

slides.title: From an interrupt request to a handler
slides.caption: Figure 6.1: PIC and vector table on MS-DOS; APIC, IDT, filters and interrupt threads on FreeBSD
slides.notes: Trace IRQ1 on both lanes. On MS-DOS any program can rewrite the vector; the handler runs on the interrupted program's time. On FreeBSD only drivers install handlers, and the work is split into a filter that runs at once and a thread that is scheduled. Ask why vector 8 cannot be IRQ0 in protected mode: it is the double fault.

slides.title: Reading the CMOS clock on MS-DOS: ports 70h and 71h
slides.code:
cli
        push    bx
        push    ax                      ;save user NMI state
        or      al,NMI                  ;disable NMI for us
        out     CMOS_PORT,al
        nop                             ;undocumented delay needed
        in      al,CMOS_DATA            ;get data value

         ;set NMI state to user specified
        mov     bx,ax                   ;save data value
        pop     ax                      ;get user NMI
        and     al,NMI
        or      al,CMOS_SHUT_DOWN
        out     CMOS_PORT,al
        nop
        in      al,CMOS_DATA
callouts: CLI: one CPU, one program, enough
Bit 7 of the index masks NMI
slides.notes: This is CMOS_READ in IO.SYS. Point out the undocumented delay and the NMI bit. MS-DOS uses this only to repair the RTC rate registers on early ATs; for time it asks the BIOS.

slides.title: The same chip from FreeBSD's atrtc driver
callouts: Callers hold the spin mutex atrtc_lock
slides.notes: Put this next to the previous slide. The protocol is identical; the locking is not: a spin mutex disables interrupts on this CPU and keeps the others out.

slides.title: The MS-DOS device driver chain after boot
slides.caption: Figure 6.3: NUL first, DEVICE= drivers after it, BCON and BCLOCK pointers in the List of Lists

slides.title: DOS writes console characters with INT 29h
slides.code:
PUSH    DS
        LDS     BX,[SI.sf_devptr]               ; output to special?
        TEST    BYTE PTR [BX+SDEVATT],ISSPEC
        POP     DS
        JZ      RAWNORM                         ; if not, do normally
        INT     int_fastcon                     ; quickly output the char
RAWRET:
        CLC
RAWRET1:
        POP     BX
        return
RAWNORM:
        CALL    RAWOUT3
        JMP     RAWRET
callouts: Is standard output a special device?
slides.notes: RAWOUT is where the console output of functions 01h-0Ch ends. The special bit (bit 4) means the device owns INT 29h. This is why ANSI.SYS must hook vector 29h; a device without the bit, or a file when output is redirected, is reached through IOFUNC instead.

slides.title: The ANSI.SYS escape-sequence state machine
slides.code:
VIDEO:  MOV     SI,OFFSET STATE
        JMP     [SI]

S2:     CMP     AL,'['
        JZ      S22
        JMP     S1
S22:    MOV     WORD PTR [SI],OFFSET S3
        XOR     BX,BX
        MOV     WORD PTR INQ,BX
        JMP     SHORT S3B

S3:     CMP     AL,';'
        JNZ     S3C
S3A:    INC     PRMCNT
S3B:    CALL    GETPTR
        XOR     AX,AX
        MOV     WORD PTR [BX],AX    ;DEFAULT VALUE IS ZERO
        RET
callouts: STATE holds the address of the current state
slides.notes: Show Lab 6.4 next: the same file with and without the driver. Mention the two features that write into the keyboard stream: the cursor report and key reassignment.

slides.title: Programs that bypass DOS
bullets: Speed: one REP MOVSW into B800h versus a long call chain per character
No redirection: INT 10h and B800h never pass a handle (Lab 6.1)
No arbitration: the last program to hook a vector wins (the INT 1Ch story)
Later systems had to emulate the hardware: EMM386 traps ports in V86 mode
FreeBSD: IN and OUT fault; /dev/io is a controlled exception
slides.notes: Use the BASCOM comment in MSBIO1.ASM as the story. Be fair: on a 4.77 MHz 8088 these shortcuts were what made software usable.

slides.title: FreeBSD: buses, drivers, interrupts
slides.subtitle: newbus, bus_space, interrupt threads
slides.notes: No BIOS after boot: the kernel finds the devices itself.

slides.title: Part of the newbus device tree
slides.caption: Figure 6.4: each box is a device_t; drivers bid in probe, the winner attaches
slides.notes: Compare with the DOS chain: a flat list loaded on command versus a tree discovered by buses. Resources come from the parent bus and are recorded, so two drivers cannot own the same port.

slides.title: Filters run now; handlers run in a thread
callouts: A handler without a filter means: schedule the thread
slides.notes: atrtc installs a filter, atkbd a threaded handler. On x86 the EOI is sent before the thread runs; a level-triggered source is also masked until the thread has run, an edge-triggered one such as IRQ1 is not.

slides.title: Cooked and raw input on both systems
slides.caption: Figure 6.5: the line editor runs when DOS reads; the line discipline runs when the key arrives
slides.notes: Raw mode is per SFT entry on MS-DOS, per terminal on FreeBSD; neither is per process.

slides.title: DOS_READ on a device: raw or cooked
slides.code:
;
; We need to hit the device.  Figure out if we do a raw read or we do the
; bizarre std_con_string_input.
;
TESTRAW:
        TEST    BL,devid_device_raw     ; Raw mode?
        JNZ     DVRDRAW                 ; Yes, let the device do all local editing
        TEST    BL,devid_device_con_in  ; Is it console device?
        JZ      NOTRDCON
        JMP     READCON
callouts: Bit 5 of the device information: raw
Raw: one request for the full count
Cooked console: the line editor of function 0Ah
slides.notes: IOCTL 4401h sets this bit. Run Lab 6.3 step 3 live: Ctrl-C, Ctrl-S and Ctrl-Z arrive as bytes.

slides.title: MS-DOS CON versus the FreeBSD terminal
rows: SIGINT to the foreground group at once
slides.notes: Two Ctrl-Zs: end of file on DOS, suspend on FreeBSD.

slides.title: Time: a count of interrupts versus a counter
bullets: MS-DOS: the BIOS counts IRQ0 ticks (18.2 Hz); CLOCK$ converts ticks to h:m:s.hh
IO.SYS reads only the date from the CMOS clock at boot
A lost interrupt makes the DOS clock late; two missed midnights lose a day
FreeBSD: the RTC once at boot (inittodr), then a timecounter (TSC; Hyper-V-TSC in the course VM)
time = timehands offset + scale x counter delta, often computed in user space
slides.notes: Show Lab 6.2's output: four readings of the same clock. DOSBox-X's CMOS held UTC.

---- THREE  (to) OUT.TXT

---- SCREEN

slides.title: Lab 6.2: the clock read four ways
bullets: INT 21h 2Ah/2Ch: binary, from CLOCK$
INT 1Ah 04h/02h and ports 70h/71h: BCD from the chip
Register A 26h, B 03h: 24-hour, BCD
All one hour behind the host: DOSBox-X's CMOS held UTC
slides.notes: Ask students to redo the tick conversion by hand with the formula in MSCLOCK.ASM.

slides.title: Lab 6.3: cooked, raw, and a sticky end of file
slides.text:
handle 0 switched to raw
handle 0: DX=C0F3 ISDEV NOTEOF RAW SPECL ISCOT ISCIN
handle 1: DX=80C0 ISDEV NOTEOF
handle 2: DX=C0F3 ISDEV NOTEOF RAW SPECL ISCOT ISCIN
read returned 0009h bytes: 61 62 08 63 0D 1A 03 13 71

After a Ctrl-Z in a previous program:
---- STUFF hi^M
---- KEYS
handle 0: DX=C093 ISDEV SPECL ISCOT ISCIN
handle 1: DX=80C0 ISDEV NOTEOF
handle 2: DX=C093 ISDEV SPECL ISCOT ISCIN
cooked read(0, buf, 40)
read returned 0000h bytes:
slides.notes: Raw: nine keys, nine bytes. The second part is the surprise: the end-of-file bit lives in the shared SFT entry of CON and only a write through it resets it.

slides.title: Lab 6.4: ANSI.SYS
bullets: Without the driver, ESC is printed as a glyph
With it, cursor moves and colours work
ESC[97;"hello"p: typing a now types hello
ESC[6n: the reply arrives as keyboard input
FreeBSD's emulator has the reply code under #if 0: the VM console never answers
slides.notes: The key reassignment is the memorable part: a text file changed the keyboard.

slides.title: Lab 6.5: the driver chain, walked from NUL
slides.text:
# header     attr strat intr  name      flags
  1 02C1:0048 8004 18DB  18E1  NUL       char NUL
  2 0BA3:0000 C053 00C1  00CC  CON       char STDIN STDOUT INT29 IOCTL GENIOCTL
  3 0070:016E 8013 062A  0635  CON       char STDIN STDOUT INT29
  4 0070:0180 8000 062A  063B  AUX       char
  5 0070:0192 A040 062A  0658  PRN       char OUTBUSY GENIOCTL
  6 0070:01A4 8008 062A  067E  CLOCK$    char CLOCK
  7 0070:01B6 0842 062A  0684  2 units   block 32BIT OPCL GENIOCTL
  8 0070:01CA 8000 062A  063B  COM1      char
slides.notes: All IO.SYS drivers share the strategy routine at 062A; AUX and COM1 even share an interrupt entry. ANSI.SYS's CON comes first.

slides.title: Labs 6.6 and 6.7: FreeBSD drivers and termios
bullets: grep DRIVER_MODULE: the same driver registers with isa and acpi
devinfo -u in the VM: the classic ports and IRQs, each with its driver
tcsetattr is ioctl(TIOCSETA = 0x802c7414) in the real libc.so.7
The VM has atkbd0 and Hyper-V's hvkbd0; console keys come through hvkbd0
rawkeys -r on the console: 61 62 08 63 0D 1A 03 13 71, as on MS-DOS
slides.notes: All outputs were captured in the course VM. rawkeys on the vt console: canonical 61 63 0A; raw 61 62 08 63 0D 1A 03 13 71, the same nine bytes as MS-DOS in Lab 6.3 (Backspace sends 08 on vt). In vmstat -i, irq1: atkbd0 does not move when you type on the Hyper-V console; the cpuN:hyperv lines do.

slides.title: Key takeaways
bullets: Same chips, same ports, same IRQs; different rules about who may touch them
MS-DOS layers are conventions; FreeBSD layers are enforced
DOS drivers: a header, a packet, a chain; FreeBSD: newbus, kobj methods, resources
Console input: polled and edited on demand versus processed on arrival
Time: counting interrupts versus reading a counter
slides.notes: Close by asking which design choice students would keep for a small embedded system today.
